pr_comments: It's ignored - good point, I'll make sure that's in the docstring

>> How does `format="ISO8601"` interact with `exact=True/False`?
>
> It's ignored - good point, I'll make sure that's in the docstring

Could we raise an error instead? (since the default is OK, it's only when the user explicitly passes `exact=False` that this can occur, so an error if you pass both `format="ISO8601", exact=False` seems fine?)

One question that is not directly clear to me from the doc update (without diving into the code): you can pass `format="ISO8601"` explicitly, but do we also "infer" this format? (i.e. if the inferred format is a subset of ISO8601, use the flexible one as inferred format) 

I assume not (and we probably also wouldn't want to do that, I think? Although it would be more backwards compatible), but I was wondering if we can make this clearer for the cases that would benefit from this (like `pd.to_datetime(["2022-01-01T09:00:00", "2022-01-02T09:00:00.123"])`) that work fine on pandas < 2, but error now. 
Right now, that case gives a "... doesn't match format ..." error message. _Ideally_ we could point people to this option. In theory we could check if the inferred format is ISO-like and infer the format from the non-matching string, and if that is also ISO like, append the error message. But that's maybe making it a bit too complicated not worth this corner case ;)

> but do we also "infer" this format? (i.e. if the inferred format is a subset of ISO8601, use the flexible one as inferred format)
> I assume not 

I wasn't planning on doing that, as it would strike me as value-dependent behaviour

Good point on the error message though, probably worth putting extra effort in to making sure that's as clear and actionable as possible

Thanks for your review!

1. it'll still try the ISO8601 fastpath first, so it shouldn't be a loss in performance. However, they will no longer get the validation that the elements are all ISO8601 - e.g. if they had an element that was %Y-%d-%m, then `to_datetime(..., format='mixed')` would parse it, whereas `format='ISO8601'` wouldn't
2. that's right, this doesn't affect non-string inputs

issue_context.title: API allow for `format='mixed'` in to_datetime
issue_context.body:
This was brought up in the community call.

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/50939 adds support for mixed ISO8601 strings. But people may have mixed not-necessarily-ISO8601 strings, and want them parsed in a more performant manner than `apply`.

So, `format='mixed'` could accomplish that. This would risk parsing `['12/01/2000', '13/01/2000']` in different formats, but because users have to opt-in to it by explicitly writing `format='mixed'`, then it should be clear to them that they will need to accept whatever risks come from this. In any case, they can always use `dayfirst`.

Alternatives would be to add a new keyword argument, or un-deprecate `infer_datetime_format` and change its behaviour. However:
- bringing back `infer_datetime_format` but changing behaviour might be confusing
- mixed non-ISO formats in a large dataset strikes me a pretty unusual use-case, and not one that would justify extra keyword arguments

Docs and error messages should be updated to direct users towards this option

It's probably easiest to tackle this as part of #50939
comments:
Just adding for future reference as argument for allowing this: currently we point people towards using `apply(pd.to_datetime)` if you have mixed strings and want to parse element-wise. But the overhead of calling `pd.to_datetime` on scalars is really _huge_. A small example:

```python
s = pd.Series(["12 Jan 2000", "2000-01-13"]*50_000)

# using pandas 1.5
In [2]: %timeit pd.to_datetime(s)
5.41 ms ± 56.7 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)

# using current main
In [2]: %time s.apply(pd.to_datetime)
CPU times: user 40 s, sys: 16.1 ms, total: 40 s
Wall time: 40.1 s

# with the open PR
In [3]: %timeit pd.to_datetime(s, format="mixed")
6.76 ms ± 423 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```

review_comments: It's true that in that case that is best, but the typicaly caveat of that this `dayfirst=True/False` is not strict still applies, right?

true, but it would solve the typical example at least
```python
In [2]: pd.to_datetime(['12-01-2000 00:00:00', '13-01-2000 00:00:00'], format='mixed', dayfirst=True)
Out[2]: DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-12', '2000-01-13'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
```
Yes, I was just wondering if it would be useful to still call it out here explicitly (but it's quite explicit in the `dayfirst` entry in the docstring)
Would making `format` default to `mixed` be "less" API breaking behavior compared to what `to_datetime` did in 1.5?

Yes, I did consider it, but then realised it would bring back the decade-long bug which PDEP4 was meant to address 😄 
```python
In [10]: to_datetime(['12/01/2000 00:00', '13/01/2000 00:00'])
Out[10]: DatetimeIndex(['2000-12-01', '2000-01-13'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
```

The US is the only country in the world to use month-first, so a default with `format='mixed'` and `dayfirst=False` results in unexpected behaviour for people in the vast majority of the world

I'm OK with allowing flexible parsing, but really think it should be opt-in
